Calculator Methodology

The formulas behind each calculator, written out so you can check the maths.

TDEE and maintenance calories

We estimate basal metabolic rate (BMR) with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, then multiply by an activity factor to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE).

MenBMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5
WomenBMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age − 161
Activity factorsSedentary 1.2 · Light 1.375 · Moderate 1.55 · Very active 1.725 · Extra active 1.9
TDEE page targetsMild cut −200 · Aggressive cut −400 · Lean bulk +250 · Aggressive bulk +400 kcal/day

Macros

The macros calculator starts from the same TDEE and applies a goal factor: × 1.12 to build muscle, × 1.00 to maintain and × 0.82 to lose fat. Protein is set at 2.0 g per kg of bodyweight (2.2 g/kg when losing fat) and fat at 1.0 g per kg. Carbohydrates fill the remaining calories at 4 kcal per gram. Protein and carbohydrates provide 4 kcal per gram and fat 9 kcal per gram.

BMI

BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². We use the standard adult categories: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, 30 and above obese.

Unit conversions

Pounds are converted at about 2.205 lb per kilogram and feet-and-inches at 2.54 cm per inch. Switching units in a calculator converts your current values for you.

Limitations

  • Equations estimate averages; individual energy expenditure varies by 10–15% or more.
  • Activity level is the biggest source of error — most people overestimate it.
  • The macros calculator displays at least 50 g of carbohydrate, which can nudge totals slightly above target at very low calories.
  • BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and is unreliable for athletes, older adults and under-18s.
  • These tools are not medical advice. Use them as a starting point and adjust from real-world results.

Try them: TDEE calculator, macros calculator, BMI calculator.
